strengths: Addresses an important and timely NLP problem: multi-hop claim verification requires tightly coupled reasoning and iterative evidence seeking, and the paper motivates this interdependence clearly.

The HARIS architecture is coherent and intuitive: a high-level reasoning agent constructs verification chains and issues questions, while a specialized low-level search agent iteratively retrieves and refines evidence.
The training procedure is described in substantial detail, including GRPO, retrieved-token loss masking, reward design, rollout formats, and alternating coordination between the two agents.

The empirical evaluation covers multiple hop settings on HOVER and EX-FEVER, includes several strong baselines, and reports ablations for the multi-agent design and number of coordination rounds. The 4B model's results are encouraging.
Qualitative examples help illustrate how the reasoning and search agents interact and adapt queries based on partial evidence.
The appendix improves reproducibility by providing dataset details, retrieval settings, hyperparameters, hardware, prompt templates, DSPy signatures, and synthesized training examples.
weaknesses: The claim of fully end-to-end training with outcome-based rewards and no intermediate supervision is overstated. The search agent is trained using GPT-4o-generated pseudo ground-truth answers derived from gold evidence and a GPT-4o-mini judge; these are intermediate QA-level supervisory signals. The agents are also optimized alternately rather than through one fully differentiable end-to-end objective.

Headline comparisons do not fully isolate the contribution. HARIS receives 7,200 in-domain training examples, whereas most GPT-4o baselines appear to use in-context prompting; backbone sizes and systems also differ. Although Table 2 includes an RL-trained single-agent comparison, the main Table 1 results conflate architecture, model choice, and in-domain training.

The retrieval protocol is inconsistent or insufficiently specified: Section 4.3 states that all methods use the same Wikipedia top-3 corpus, but FOLK is described as using the Google Search API/SerpAPI. Search budgets and maximum agent calls should also be matched and explicitly reported.

Statistical evidence is limited. Results are based on 500 sampled instances per setting, with no random seeds, error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Several gains are small, and HARIS ties Search-o1 exactly on HOVER 2-hop F1 and accuracy. The definition and label averaging of the reported F1 score are also unclear.

The LLM-as-a-Judge versus F1 ablation reports only training-call and reward curves, not final downstream verification performance. Moreover, higher judge reward for a judge-trained model is partly circular. There is no direct evaluation of retrieval precision/recall, query refinement, evidence-chain correctness, or human-rated evidence quality.

The CHECKWHY generalization evaluation is underdeveloped: only positive samples are used, the label setup is not fully explained, and only accuracy is reported. This is insufficient for the strong generalization claim made in the results section.

The conceptual novelty is somewhat incremental relative to prior agentic RAG, search-augmented reasoning, and RL-trained search agents. The main advance is the particular hierarchical and coordinated training design rather than a fundamentally new reasoning or retrieval mechanism.

Scope and reproducibility remain limited: experiments are restricted to binary English Wikipedia claims, neutral/insufficient-information labels are excluded, and only a 4B model is trained. I did not see a code-release commitment, evaluation seeds, raw model outputs, or complete judge prompts/rubrics.
The paper would benefit from polishing: there are typographical errors such as 'colloraborate' and 'Comparision,' a spacing error in 'capability.A,' and duplicated text in Sections B.1 and B.2.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and highly relevant NLP problem: multi-hop claim verification requires tightly coupling iterative evidence retrieval with multi-step reasoning rather than treating them as separate stages.

The proposed high-level reasoning agent and low-level search agent are intuitive and modular. The use of explicit question, result, search, report, and verification tags makes the interaction relatively transparent and gives the system potentially useful traceability.

The same-backbone comparison in Table 2 between an RL-trained single agent and HARIS is the most convincing experiment. HARIS improves performance on most settings, with particularly noticeable gains on the harder HOVER 4-hop subset.

The empirical evaluation includes two standard multi-hop benchmarks, EX-FEVER and HOVER, and attempts an out-of-domain evaluation on CHECKWHY. The appendix also provides prompt templates, DSPy signatures, retrieval settings, and major hyperparameters.

The case studies concretely illustrate the intended behavior: the reasoning agent can disambiguate entities and revise its path based on intermediate evidence, while the search agent refines queries instead of issuing only one static retrieval request.
The synthesis of search-agent training data from questions produced by the reasoning agent is a practical way to align the two agents’ interaction styles.
weaknesses: The central claim that coordinated training is the key source of improvement is not adequately identified. The direct comparison between N=1 and N=3 reports small and sometimes inconsistent gains; for example, HOVER 4-hop F1 and accuracy decrease from 60.87/61.80 to 59.84/61.00. There are no confidence intervals or significance tests, and missing controls include independently trained agents, frozen agents, unidirectional updates, and equal retrieval budgets.

The main baseline comparison is confounded. HARIS is a Qwen3-4B model trained with RL, whereas most baselines are prompted GPT-4o systems; Search-o1 uses a QwQ-32B model, and FOLK uses a different Google Search API. Differences in backbone size, training, retrieval implementation, and search budget make it difficult to attribute the results specifically to the proposed architecture.

The evaluation uses only 500 sampled instances per hop setting rather than the full test sets. The paper does not report seeds, confidence intervals, bootstrap results, or statistical significance. The F1 metric is also not clearly defined as macro-F1, label-F1, or another variant.

The CHECKWHY evaluation is limited to positive samples and reports only accuracy. Because the system is not tested on the negative or counterfactual cases, this result does not establish the ability to discriminate false claims, and the claimed generalization to causally structured verification is therefore weak.

The search-agent reward depends on GPT-4o-generated pseudo ground-truth answers and a GPT-4o-mini judge, but neither the pseudo labels nor the judge’s reliability is validated against human judgments. Verbosity bias, answer-style bias, and reward hacking are not analyzed. Moreover, this is not a fully end-to-end outcome-based reward: the search agent is rewarded for intermediate QA usefulness rather than for whether its evidence leads to the correct final verdict.

The paper claims improved interpretability and search-informed reasoning, but it only evaluates final Support/Refute decisions. There is no systematic evaluation of question quality, report relevance, evidence precision or recall, chain correctness, or hallucination. The qualitative examples are illustrative but cannot substitute for such an analysis.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The manuscript does not state whether code, trained checkpoints, synthesized training data, or evaluation samples will be released. It also omits inference-time search-call statistics, total retrieved-document budgets, latency and monetary cost, several GPT generation settings, and random seeds. Algorithm 1 is ambiguous about the distinction between epochs and coordination rounds and about which agent is frozen during each update.

The technical novelty is somewhat incremental relative to prior agentic RAG, search-reasoning RL, and multi-agent verification systems. The alternating coordination procedure is the main new element, but its advantage over ordinary sequential training and prior search-agent methods is not sharply isolated. The abstract’s claim that HARIS ‘greatly advances’ the field is stronger than the evidence supports.

The presentation would benefit from polishing: there are typographical errors such as ‘colloraborate’ and ‘Comparision’, a missing space in ‘verification capability.A’, and near-duplicated paragraphs in Sections B.1 and B.2.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and challenging problem in multi-hop claim verification: the bidirectional interplay between reasoning-guided search and search-informed reasoning. The motivating example clearly motivates why static decomposition or single-pass retrieval is insufficient.

HARIS provides a clean and intuitive architecture. Separating the high-level verification/reasoning agent from the low-level iterative search agent allows each model to specialize, while the tag-based question/result interface makes their interaction interpretable and traceable.

The coordinated GRPO training procedure is described in reasonable detail, including agent rollouts, reward functions, retrieved-token masking, alternating optimization, retrieval settings, prompts, and synthesized training examples. This makes the core approach substantially reproducible.

The empirical results are strong across HOVER and EX-FEVER, including more difficult 3-hop and 4-hop settings. HARIS also outperforms the matched RL-trained single-agent baseline in Table 2, which is the most direct evidence for the claimed benefit of role specialization.

The paper includes useful ablations on coordination rounds, reward design, and single- versus multi-agent behavior, together with qualitative rollouts that illustrate how search can redirect reasoning when the initial entity or evidence path is ambiguous.

The work is clearly written and highly relevant to NLP, fact verification, retrieval-augmented generation, and LLM agent training. The 4B trained model performing competitively with much larger or GPT-4o-based systems is practically appealing.
weaknesses: The statistical rigor of the evaluation is limited. Results are reported on 500 sampled instances per setting without confidence intervals, significance tests, or multiple training seeds. Some gains, especially on HOVER 2-hop, are small and could be unstable.

The coordination-round ablation does not consistently support the claim that more rounds improve performance. In Table 3, N=3 is worse than N=1 on HOVER 2-hop F1 and on both HOVER 4-hop metrics. With only N=1 and N=3 compared, the evidence for iterative co-training is suggestive rather than conclusive.

The description of HARIS as trained 'end-to-end' with purely outcome-based rewards is somewhat overstated. The search agent receives GPT-4o-generated pseudo ground-truth answers and an LLM-as-a-judge utility score for intermediate questions, which is a form of intermediate supervision rather than reward directly derived from the final claim decision.

The LLM-as-a-judge reward is not adequately validated. The paper compares training dynamics but does not report held-out performance, agreement with human judgments, judge bias, or sensitivity to the GPT-4o-mini judge. This matters because the judge can reward plausible but unsupported evidence.

Evaluation details need more clarification. F1 is not explicitly defined for the binary setting, and the CHECKWHY evaluation uses only 'positive' samples, making the label distribution and meaning of the 60.80 accuracy unclear. Additional label-wise results would make the claims more convincing.

Although the main results are strong, system-level comparison is not perfectly controlled: HARIS is a fine-tuned 4B model, most baselines use GPT-4o, and Search-o1 uses a different 32B model. The matched single-agent ablation is valuable, but a same-size untrained or supervised baseline would further strengthen attribution.

The novelty is incremental relative to prior agentic retrieval and RL-search systems such as Search-o1, Search-R1, R1-searcher, and decomposition-based verifiers. The precise technical distinction from simply combining a search-enabled reasoner with multi-agent decomposition should be sharpened.

Reproducibility would be improved by explicitly releasing code and model checkpoints and by providing training steps, sampling temperatures, exact judge prompts, latency/search-cost comparisons, and random seeds. There are also minor presentation issues, including duplicated Appendix B.1/B.2 text, 'Comparision' in Figure 4, and a missing space in Section 5.2.

The limitations section is narrow. It does not thoroughly discuss retrieval corpus dependence, exposure to missing evidence or NEI-style labels, annotation/pseudo-answer noise, computational cost, or failure cases where the two agents may reinforce an incorrect reasoning path.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: the recursive coupling of reasoning-guided query generation and search-informed evidence refinement in multi-hop claim verification.

The HARIS architecture and coordinated training procedure are technically coherent and well specified. The separation of high-level reasoning and low-level search agents, tag-based interaction protocol, reward design, GRPO objective, retrieved-token masking, and foundation/alternating training stages are clearly described.

The empirical evaluation is comparatively broad, covering EX-FEVER, HOVER, hop-count subsets, and CHECKWHY, together with ablations for single-agent versus multi-agent designs, coordination rounds, reward functions, supervised fine-tuning, ReAct, and model scaling.

The same-base-model comparison in Appendix B and the RL-trained single-agent comparison help isolate the benefit of specialization from simply using a stronger or fine-tuned model. Improvements are especially pronounced on the harder 3-hop and 4-hop settings.

The paper provides useful interpretability through complete agent traces and includes substantial reproducibility material in the appendices, such as prompts, DSPy signatures, hyperparameters, training-data examples, and human-evaluation details.
weaknesses: The novelty is somewhat incremental relative to closely related work, particularly BiDeV, which already uses cooperative reasoning/search agents and joint RL training, as well as Search-o1 and other agentic-RAG systems. The paper does not sharply isolate which HARIS component—hierarchical delegation, alternating training, or the LLM-judge reward—causes the gains.

The headline Table 1 mixes models, training regimes, and retrieval infrastructures: HARIS is a task-trained Qwen3-4B system, whereas most baselines use prompted GPT-4o, Search-o1 uses a 32B model, and FOLK uses Google Search grounding. The Qwen3-4B table in the appendix mitigates this concern, but the primary comparison remains potentially misleading.

Results are reported as point estimates on 500 stratified samples per setting, without confidence intervals, significance tests, multiple seeds, or full test-set evaluation. Several 2-hop improvements are small and may not be statistically reliable.

Training depends heavily on GPT-4o-generated pseudo-ground-truth answers and GPT-4o-mini LLM-as-a-judge rewards. Although the human-evaluation study is valuable, it covers only 150 synthesized search questions and does not directly validate downstream verification decisions, leaving concerns about judge bias and reward hacking.
Reproducibility would be improved by filling in the currently blank code link and releasing data splits, sampled instance IDs, seeds, model checkpoints, and complete evaluation scripts.

The paper lacks systematic analysis of retrieval failures, agent error modes, latency, number of search calls, and computational cost. The CHECKWHY evaluation uses only positive samples, and the binary-label/4B-model scope limits the strength of the broader generalization claims.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and highly relevant NLP problem: multi-hop claim verification requires iterative evidence discovery as well as reasoning, and the hierarchical two-agent design makes the verification chain and information requests inspectable.

The coordinated training recipe is technically coherent: foundation training followed by alternating GRPO updates, on-policy question synthesis from the current reasoning agent, and retrieved-token loss masking to stabilize policy learning.

The empirical evaluation is broad, covering HOVER and EX-FEVER across multiple hop counts, an out-of-domain CHECKWHY evaluation, strong recent baselines, and ablations for agent decomposition, coordination rounds, reward design, supervised finetuning, and model scale.

The results support the intended benefit especially on harder reasoning chains: gains are largest on 3- and 4-hop HOVER, and the same-backbone comparison shows substantial improvements over Qwen3-4B baselines in that setting.
The appendix improves reproducibility by providing prompt templates, DSPy signatures, hyperparameters, hardware details, and examples of synthesized training data.
weaknesses: The claim of end-to-end training with outcome-based rewards and no intermediate supervision is overstated. The search agent is optimized against pseudo ground-truth answers generated from gold evidence and an intermediate LLM-as-a-Judge score; alternating optimization is not a single end-to-end objective.

The headline comparison is confounded by heterogeneous systems: HARIS is an in-domain-trained Qwen3-4B model, most baselines use prompted GPT-4o, Search-o1 uses QwQ-32B, and FOLK uses Google Search API. The same-backbone Table 5 is therefore essential, but it reports exact ties with FOLK on both EX-FEVER settings, so broad superiority is not established under a controlled retriever and backbone setup.

There is no uncertainty or significance analysis. Evaluation uses 500 sampled instances per setting, apparently one training run, and no confidence intervals, bootstrap tests, or repeated seeds. Several main-table improvements are under one point and could reflect sampling or RL variance.

The coordination-round ablation confounds mutual adaptation with additional optimization: N=3 receives more training updates than N=1, but there is no control condition receiving the same number of independent updates.

Reward validity depends heavily on generated labels and model judges. GPT-4o creates pseudo answers while GPT-4o-mini scores evidence usefulness, creating risks of circularity, reward hacking, and bias toward verbose outputs. The human audit covers only 150 synthetic questions, and Appendix D is unclear about whether the reported kappa is LLM-versus-human or human-versus-human agreement.

Foundation search training uses ground-truth evidence to construct answers, whereas testing relies on noisy top-3 retrieved chunks. This train/test distribution gap and the method's sensitivity to retrieval errors are not quantitatively analyzed.

The generalization and efficiency evidence is limited. CHECKWHY uses only positive samples, so it does not assess refutational decisions, and the paper does not compare inference latency, token usage, or the number of search calls against baselines.

There is no quantitative error analysis of HARIS itself. The qualitative examples are favorable and largely illustrate successful cases or a single-agent failure, but do not categorize HARIS retrieval misses, reasoning errors, or remaining failure modes.

The code footnote appears empty in the supplied manuscript. Reproducibility would be strengthened by releasing code, sample identifiers, seeds, synthetic data, and checkpoints, as well as clarifying the exact F1 definition. The duplicated C.2/C.3 text and several typographical errors should also be corrected.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and highly relevant problem in computational linguistics: multi-hop claim verification requiring iterative evidence discovery and evidence-conditioned reasoning.

The two-level design is well motivated and interpretable. The high-level agent constructs the verification chain and poses factual questions, while the low-level agent iteratively retrieves and refines evidence through a structured tag-based interaction protocol.

The coordinated GRPO training procedure is reasonably complete and technically coherent. It includes foundation and alternating-training stages, role-specific rewards, retrieved-token loss masking, and a clear algorithmic description.

Results are consistent across HOVER and EX-FEVER and are especially strong on harder 3-hop and 4-hop settings. The positive CHECKWHY result also provides some evidence of transfer beyond the main benchmarks.

The paper includes several useful ablations: multi-agent versus single-agent, coordination rounds, LLM-as-a-judge versus F1-style rewards, same-backbone comparison, supervised fine-tuning, and ReAct scaling. The human evaluation of the LLM judge, with Cohen's kappa of 0.81 and 93.3% agreement, is also valuable.
The appendices substantially support reproducibility through prompt templates, DSPy signatures, hyperparameters, hardware details, synthesized-data examples, and qualitative agent trajectories.
weaknesses: The main experimental comparison is not fully controlled. Table 1 compares in-domain RL-trained Qwen3-4B HARIS with mostly GPT-4o-based baselines and a QwQ-32B Search-o1 system. Table 5 is therefore necessary and should be emphasized more, but even there retrieval sources and training resources differ; for example, HARIS exactly ties FOLK on both EX-FEVER settings. Paired significance tests, confidence intervals, and multiple training seeds are missing.

The claim that HARIS is trained end-to-end without intermediate supervision is overstated. The search agent uses synthetic questions from reasoning rollouts, GPT-4o-generated pseudo ground-truth answers, an auxiliary LLM-as-a-judge reward, and format rewards. The agents are also updated alternately rather than jointly. This is coordinated multi-policy RL with auxiliary pseudo-supervision, not purely end-to-end final-outcome training.

The method depends heavily on closed-model teachers: GPT-4o generates pseudo answers and GPT-4o-mini provides search rewards. The human validation covers only 150 synthesized questions and does not directly establish that the judge is robust on held-out claim-verification trajectories or immune to verbosity bias and reward hacking.

Evaluation rigor is limited by using 500 stratified samples per setting without releasing sample identifiers, reporting policy variance across seeds, or defining whether F1 is macro- or micro-averaged. The binary support/refute setting and positive-only CHECKWHY subset also constrain the scope of the conclusions.

Generality and robustness are not fully established. HARIS itself is trained only at the 4B scale and evaluated against a static Wikipedia corpus with top-3 retrieval. The ReAct scaling experiment does not test whether HARIS remains effective at 8B or 14B, and there is no quantitative breakdown of retrieval failures, reasoning failures, latency, token cost, or search-call efficiency.

Although the integration is solid, the individual components are somewhat incremental relative to prior agentic RAG, GRPO-based search systems, and dual-agent verification frameworks such as Search-o1, Search-R1, BiDeV, LoCal, and RAG-gym. A more direct comparison against independently trained agents or a shared-reward multi-agent baseline would better isolate the contribution of alternating coordination.

The code-availability footnote appears incomplete in the manuscript, with no visible repository URL. Releasing code, random seeds, sampled evaluation IDs, prompt versions, and decoding settings would make the substantially detailed experimental setup easier to reproduce.
